question: A colleague proposes doubling the number of rollout engines, each still decoding a share of one synchronous batch, to fix 51% engine idleness. What is the main flaw?
options: More engines need more weight-sync bandwidth, which is the real bottleneck
Doubling engines doubles the length of every response
Engines cannot run in parallel on one batch
The idle time is set by the longest response, and one response cannot be split across engines, so the phase still lasts as long as that response
explain: Autoregressive decoding of one response is sequential. Adding engines shortens the time to finish the short responses, but the phase still waits for the longest one, so idleness goes up. verl's fully async docs make the same point: in the colocated case, adding rollout resources cannot remove long-tail idleness.

courseTitle: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
lessonTitle: Why a kernel is limited by its slowest resource
question: A kernel does 2 GFLOP and moves 4 GB on an H100 (989.5 TFLOP/s BF16, 3.35 TB/s). Which change would speed it up the most?
options: Fusing it with the next kernel so its output never goes to DRAM
Switching from BF16 to FP8 Tensor Cores to double the math rate
Raising the SM clock to increase peak FLOP/s
Unrolling the inner loop to improve instruction level parallelism
explain: Math time is 2 GFLOP / 989.5 TFLOP/s = 2 us, memory time is 4 GB / 3.35 TB/s = 1,194 us. The kernel is memory bound, so only cutting bytes (fusion keeps intermediates on chip) helps. Every option that speeds up math leaves the 1,194 us untouched.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: Walking the dependency graph to the anomalous frontier
question: Pricing is anomalous and so is catalog, which pricing calls. A junior engineer proposes rolling back pricing, since pricing is where the user-visible errors are counted. What does the frontier rule say?
options: Roll back pricing: it is the service returning errors, so it owns the symptom
Roll back both at once to save time
Pricing's anomaly is already explained by its anomalous dependency, so it is not a candidate until catalog is ruled out
Neither is a candidate, because both are anomalous
explain: The frontier keeps only anomalous nodes whose dependencies are healthy. Pricing's slowness is fully accounted for by waiting on catalog, and rolling back pricing changes nothing about the catalog queue while adding a second change to reason about. Rolling back both at once also destroys your ability to attribute the recovery to either one.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Why fuse ranks instead of scores
question: A new BM25 build multiplies every BM25 score by 3 (same order). What happens to the RRF-fused list?
options: Nothing: ranks are unchanged, so every RRF score is unchanged
BM25 now dominates the fusion, like the raw sum
Dense-only documents rise because BM25 is now relatively noisier
The fused list changes only if k is smaller than 3
explain: RRF reads only r(d). Any monotone transformation of one system's scores leaves its ranks, and therefore the fused list, identical. A raw score sum would change; min-max would not change in this case either, but would under a non-linear transform.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Bindings, helpers, abstractions: the layers under a Rust driver
question: A colleague's build fails: `bindings::spin_lock` does not exist even though `spin_lock()` is used all over the C code. Most likely cause?
options: The bindings crate only includes headers listed in `rust/helpers/`
Rust code may not take spinlocks
`spin_lock` is a macro or inline function in C, so bindgen emits no callable symbol; a `rust/helpers/` wrapper is needed
bindgen only runs when `CLIPPY=1` is set
explain: bindgen generates declarations for real functions and types it finds in the headers included from `rust/bindings/bindings_helper.h`. For C inline functions and non-trivial macros the docs say to add a small wrapper to `rust/helpers/`, exactly like `rust_helper_mutex_lock`.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Objects the C side owns: ARef, AlwaysRefCounted and RCU
question: Inside the scope of an `rcu::Guard`, code calls `m.lock()` on a `Mutex`. What does the Rust compiler do?
options: Accepts it. Sleeping inside an RCU read-side section is illegal, but nothing in the types tracks it; that rule needs review or a tool like klint (lesson 10)
Rejects it, because the guard borrows the mutex
Rejects it, because `Guard` is not `Send`
Accepts it, and the RCU guard is released automatically before the mutex sleeps
explain: The guard makes sure the RCU-protected *reference* does not outlive the section, but neither guard type knows about sleeping. Being `!Send` only stops the guard from moving to another thread. The kernel docs say it is illegal to block inside an RCU read-side critical section, and checking that is the job of runtime debugging or klint's atomic-context lint.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Real device drivers: probe, remove, Devres and Revocable
question: Your driver data holds `bar: pci::Bar<'bound>`. You now want a work item, which might still run after the device is unbound, to write a register. What is the sound change?
options: Store `&this.bar` in the work item; the borrow checker will extend the BAR's lifetime
Clone the `Bar` into the work item so each has its own mapping
Convert it with `bar.into_devres()` and have the work item use `try_access()`, handling `None` as an error
`transmute` the Bar to `Bar<'static>` and cancel the work item in `Drop`
explain: A work item must be `'static`, so a `&Bar<'bound>` cannot be stored in it: the borrow checker rejects it rather than extending anything. Bar is not Clone. The transmute compiles, but then soundness rests on a manual ordering rule again. A DevresBar can outlive the binding safely because every access goes through the revocation check.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Dispatch queues: how tasks travel from BPF to a CPU
question: Your enqueue callback calls scx_bpf_dsq_insert_vtime(p, SCX_DSQ_GLOBAL, slice, vtime, flags). What happens?
options: Tasks are kept in vtime order inside the global DSQ
The vtime is ignored and the task is appended FIFO
It is an error: built-in DSQs do not support priority-queue insertion, so you need a custom DSQ
The task is silently moved to the caller CPU's local DSQ
explain: Built-in DSQs (local and global) are FIFO only. The docs and scx_simple's comments say vtime insertion needs a DSQ created with scx_bpf_create_dsq(); invalid use is reported as a scheduler error, which unloads it.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Placement and preemption: idle CPUs, kicks, LOCAL_ON and locality
question: A latency-critical thread wakes while every CPU runs batch tasks with 20 ms slices. Which choice gets it running within microseconds instead of after up to 20 ms?
options: Give it a vtime lower than everyone's in the shared DSQ
Insert it into its CPU's local DSQ with SCX_ENQ_PREEMPT
Call scx_bpf_kick_cpu(cpu, SCX_KICK_IDLE) on its last CPU
Return its last CPU from select_cpu
explain: SCX_ENQ_PREEMPT zeroes the running task's slice and kicks the CPU, and the woken task is at the head of that local DSQ. A low vtime only puts it first in line for the next slice end; KICK_IDLE does nothing to a busy CPU; select_cpu's return value is a hint.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Measuring and debugging a scheduler
question: Your cpu.max test shows a cgroup capped at 50 percent using 98 percent of a CPU under scx_flatcg. What is the right conclusion?
options: usage_usec is not counted for tasks on the ext class
cpu.max applies only to SCHED_DEADLINE tasks
The test is wrong: cpu.max is always enforced by the kernel core
scx_flatcg does not implement cgroup_set_bandwidth, so the cpu.max cap is ignored while it runs
explain: The kernel passes cpu.max to the BPF scheduler through ops.cgroup_set_bandwidth(), and each scheduler chooses whether to implement it. scx_flatcg implements cpu.weight only. usage_usec is always reported, which is why it works as a check.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Revocation at scale: CircleCI and rotating every secret at once
question: After rotating 500 secrets in a hurry, what is the strongest evidence that each rotation worked?
options: Each secret's version metadata changed and a test call with the old value is refused
The rotation script exited with status 0
No alerts fired for a week
The new values are longer
explain: A script can succeed while writing to the wrong place, and silence proves nothing. Proof is two checks per secret: the store holds a new version that consumers use, and the old credential no longer authenticates.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Key hierarchies in KMS: envelope encryption and rotating the KEK
question: Why is re-wrapping 1,000 objects after a KEK rotation cheap?
options: Only each object's small wrapped DEK is decrypted and re-encrypted; the object data stays as it is
KMS caches the plaintext data
AES-GCM ciphertext can be re-keyed without decryption
Re-wrapping happens on the client GPU
explain: Envelope encryption puts a layer between data and KEK. Changing the KEK version means rewriting a few dozen bytes per object, which is why hierarchies exist.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Case: Storm-0558 and a signing key that should have died in 2021
question: Which single control would most directly have made the stolen 2016 key useless by 2023?
options: Automated rotation with enforced retirement, so the key stopped being trusted after its planned 2021 retirement
Longer RSA keys
Multi-factor authentication for users
Encrypting the mailboxes at rest
explain: The key was valid only because retirement was delayed and rotation stopped. MFA protects user logins, but forged tokens bypass the login entirely; key length does not help against theft; at-rest encryption does not stop an authorised-looking reader.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Python: eval, pickle and yaml.load turn data into code
question: Which call is safe on a YAML file uploaded by a user, with PyYAML 6?
options: `yaml.load(f, Loader=yaml.Loader)`
`yaml.unsafe_load(f)`
`yaml.safe_load(f)`
`yaml.load(f)`
explain: safe_load builds only standard types. Loader (also called UnsafeLoader) and unsafe_load can construct arbitrary Python objects. Plain yaml.load(f) raises TypeError in PyYAML 6 because the loader is required, so it is not a choice at all.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Go: nil maps, data races and the race detector
question: A Go handler stores sessions in a package-level `map[string]Session` that every request reads and some requests write, with no lock. What is the most serious consequence?
options: The map grows without limit
Each request gets its own copy, so writes are lost
Concurrent writes can stop the whole server with a fatal error, and racing reads can see corrupted state
Nothing, because Go maps are safe for concurrent use
explain: The Go FAQ says uncontrolled map access can crash the program, and our run ended with fatal error: concurrent map writes. The memory model warns races on maps can corrupt memory. Maps are shared by reference, not copied per request.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: C review checklist: strings, sizes and return values
question: `int n = snprintf(p, room, "%s", s);` returns 40 when `room` is 16. What happened?
options: snprintf wrote 40 bytes and overflowed
snprintf failed and wrote nothing
snprintf wrote 15 characters plus a terminator; 40 is the full length it wanted
The return value is undefined when truncating
explain: C's snprintf never writes more than room bytes (including the terminator) and returns the length the full output would have had. A return value of room or more is the standard signal of truncation.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Memory-safe roadmaps: CISA's guidance and Android's numbers
question: According to Android's 2024 analysis, why did the share of memory safety vulnerabilities fall while most of the code was still C and C++?
options: All old C and C++ code was rewritten in Rust
Memory safety bugs stopped being reported
Vulnerabilities concentrate in new code and decay with age, and new code was increasingly written in memory-safe languages
Compilers began rejecting all memory-unsafe code
explain: The post argues vulnerabilities have a half-life: old code becomes safer as its bugs are found, so most new bugs are in new code. Moving new development to MSLs cut the inflow, and the share fell without a full rewrite.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: IPsec building blocks: SAs, SPIs, ESP, AH and two modes
question: Paris's gateway receives an ESP packet. Which field tells it which keys to decrypt with?
options: The SPI in the ESP header, which names one security association it created
The source IP address of the outer header
The TCP destination port inside the packet
The ICV at the end of the packet
explain: The receiver picked the SPI when the SA was set up and looks it up in its SAD. The outer source address can change (NAT, roaming) and the TCP port is encrypted, so neither can be used to find the keys. The ICV is checked with the keys after they are found.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: WireGuard: one interface, public keys and cryptokey routing
question: A server's peer entry for Ana's laptop has AllowedIPs = 10.0.0.2/32. Ana's laptop is compromised and sends a tunnel packet whose inner source address is 10.0.0.1, the address of the router peer. What happens?
options: The server drops it, because 10.0.0.1 routes to a different peer than the one whose keys decrypted it
The server accepts it, because the packet decrypted correctly
The server forwards it and logs a warning
The server replies with an ICMP error to the laptop
explain: Decryption proves which peer sent the packet; the allowed-IPs check then requires the inner source to belong to that same peer. 10.0.0.1 belongs to the router's entry, so the packet is dropped.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: When the state machine forgets: Erlang/OTP SSH (CVE-2025-32433)
question: A vendor says: "We fixed it by blocking the CHANNEL_REQUEST message type before login." What is the weakness of that fix?
options: It is a blocklist; other post-authentication messages (80 and up) could still reach handlers. The robust fix allows only authentication-phase messages until login succeeds
None; CHANNEL_REQUEST is the only dangerous message
Blocking messages violates the SSH RFCs
It should block CHANNEL_OPEN instead
explain: Blocking one message type leaves every other out-of-order message reachable. RFC 4252's rule is an allow-list by state: before authentication, only the authentication protocol (and transport-layer messages) are legal.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Time is a security input: NTP, delay attacks and NTS
question: Why does an NTS server not need to store anything per client after NTS-KE?
options: The server derives each client's keys from the client's IP address
NTP has no keys, only TLS does
The client stores the session keys inside cookies that are encrypted under a key only the server knows, and sends one back with each request
The server keeps the TLS session open forever
explain: RFC 8915 puts all state on the client: each cookie carries the keys, encrypted for the server. That lets one server serve huge numbers of clients and, with fresh cookies per reply, prevents tracking a moving client.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: What security architecture is: where every control sits
question: Which of these belongs in the notes app's trusted computing base?
options: The CSS stylesheet for the login page
The marketing website on a separate host
The identity provider that signs session tokens, and the authorization middleware
Every user's laptop
explain: The TCB is what enforces the policy: if the token signer or the authorization code fails, every access decision is wrong. Stylesheets and a separate marketing site do not enforce anything. Laptops are subjects to be checked, not part of the checker.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Assurance: the Orange Book, Common Criteria and what they prove
question: A vendor says its VPN gateway is "Common Criteria EAL4 certified". What should you check first?
options: Nothing more: EAL4 means it resists skilled attackers
The security target: the TOE boundary, the evaluated configuration and the assumptions about the environment
Whether EAL4 is higher than the competitor's EAL3
Whether the vendor's website uses TLS 1.3
explain: The certificate only means the TOE described in the ST met that ST's requirements at that assurance level. If your deployment uses features outside the TOE or breaks its assumptions, the certificate says nothing about it. A higher EAL is more scrutiny of possibly different claims.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: The trust algorithm: criteria, scores and context
question: An attacker with a stolen HR account reads employee records slowly, 25 a day, during office hours, from the victim's own laptop. Which algorithm design is most likely to catch it?
options: A singular, criteria-based algorithm
A singular, score-based algorithm
A contextual algorithm that also uses other signals such as data destinations
None: zero trust cannot detect insiders at all
explain: Every request is valid alone, so singular designs allow all of them. Even the contextual record count stays normal here; SP 800-207 notes an attacker with valid credentials can still reach what the account may use. Context plus other signals (where the data goes, new behaviour) gives the best chance. It is hard, not impossible.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: SASE, SSE and the cloud edge: SD-WAN, SWG, CASB and FWaaS
question: Security wants to know which unapproved cloud file-sharing services employees use and how much data goes to each. Which component is designed for this?
options: SD-WAN
CASB
A stateful firewall
DNSSEC
explain: Discovery of cloud service use (shadow IT) was the first-generation CASB's main job, and current CASBs add data protection and policy enforcement on those services. SD-WAN routes traffic; a firewall sees addresses and ports, not services and uploads per user; DNSSEC authenticates DNS answers.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Webhooks: accepting only events you can trust
question: Your receiver lets the web framework parse the JSON, re-serialises it with json.dumps, and computes the HMAC over that string. Most genuine deliveries fail verification. Why?
options: The secret must be base64-encoded before use
HMAC cannot be computed over JSON
The sender signed the exact bytes it sent; re-serialising changes whitespace or key order, so the bytes differ
GitHub signs only the headers, not the body
explain: An HMAC is over bytes, not meaning. Keep the raw request body, verify it first, and only then parse. The other options are false: HMAC works over any bytes, GitHub signs the body, and the secret is used as given.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Case management APIs, and reading Netflix's Dispatch
question: Your worker posts A-2291 to Dispatch, the call times out, and the retry returns 409 Conflict. What should the worker do?
options: Retry with a new random id so the post succeeds
Treat it as success: the first request was stored, and the id proves it is the same alert
Delete the instance and post again
Raise an outage alert for Dispatch
explain: A 409 on a deterministic id means the earlier request landed. A new random id would create a duplicate instance; deleting and reposting loses history; nothing here suggests an outage.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Worked scenario: prompt injection through attacker-written log fields
question: Why is instruction-like text in a User-Agent header worth an alert tag of its own?
options: Legitimate clients do not address AI assistants in their headers; it suggests a person probing your tooling
It proves the attacker is a nation-state
Because the tag stops the injection from working
It is required by the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications
explain: It is a behavioural signal of a hands-on attacker who knows or guesses you use AI triage. The tag detects; it does not defend, since rephrasing evades a keyword pattern.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: What security protects: assets and the CIA triad
question: Why does a download page's published SHA-256 value not protect you if an attacker controls the whole download page?
options: SHA-256 is too short to detect changes
Hashes only protect availability
The attacker can replace both the file and the published hash, so they still match
SHA-256 can be reversed to recover the file
explain: A hash detects any change to the input, but it has no secret in it: anyone can compute it. If the same attacker supplies both the file and the expected value, they will match. That is why signed releases exist: only the real publisher can produce the signature.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: How a vulnerability becomes public: disclosure, CVE and NVD
question: Attackers exploit a flaw in a VPN appliance before the vendor knows it exists. What is this called?
options: Coordinated disclosure
A CNA
A zero-day attack
An n-day patch
explain: An attack on a previously unknown vulnerability is a zero-day attack: the vendor has had zero days to produce a fix. Coordinated disclosure is the opposite path, where the vendor hears first.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: The attack lifecycle: kill chain and MITRE ATT&CK
question: Why do defenders like the kill chain's idea that 'one mitigation breaks the chain'?
options: It means only the first phase needs defending
It means attacks are impossible
It means a detection or block at any later phase can still stop the intrusion before its objective
It means attackers must use malware
explain: Every phase is a chance to stop the attacker, so defences deep inside the network (like Equifax's traffic monitor, had it worked) still matter even after the initial break-in.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Plain, direct and first: sentences a busy reader acts on
question: Which sentence follows the plain language guidance best for a message to a service owner?
options: Your login service accepts expired session tokens; please deploy the fix in pull request 812 by Wednesday.
It is recommended that remediation of the identified issue be performed in a timely manner.
Remediation should be considered by the relevant stakeholders.
A potential weakness may exist in some authentication components.
explain: It is active, present tense, names the system, the defect, the action and the deadline. The others are passive, use hidden verbs ('remediation be performed') and leave out who and when.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Executive summaries: one page for the person who decides
question: Which sentence belongs in an executive summary?
options: An attacker on the internet can take control of the main firewall; the vendor fix takes about an hour to apply and should be applied today.
We used Nmap 7.95 and Burp Suite to enumerate the attack surface.
CVE-2024-3400 was observed on the edge firewall.
The team worked hard over two weeks.
explain: It states the consequence in business terms, the cost of fixing it and the urgency. Tool names, bare CVE numbers and effort statements belong elsewhere or nowhere.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Design-review and code-review comments that get acted on
question: Which review comment is most likely to get a correct fix quickly?
options: issue (security, blocking): /export joins a user-supplied path to the reports directory, so ../ can reach other files. Could we resolve it and check it stays inside? Helper: docs/safe-paths.md
Insecure. Fix.
Why would anyone build it like this?
nitpick: path handling
explain: It is labelled and blocking, locates the defect, gives the scenario, proposes a specific fix and points to a helper. The others give no reason, attack the author, or understate a real issue as a nitpick.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Why a model can teach itself: improve, then distill
question: Why does training the policy head on MCTS visit counts improve the network instead of just copying it?
options: Visit counts are smoother than the prior, so the cross-entropy loss is lower
The search samples at a higher temperature, so the targets are more diverse
The search mixes the prior with measured look-ahead values, so the visit counts differ from the prior where look-ahead finds better moves
The visit counts include moves from human expert games
explain: The search is an improvement operator: it starts from the prior and moves visits toward moves whose measured values are higher. In the toy, the prior said 0.30 for b and the search said 0.889. Imitating that difference is the improvement. AlphaZero uses no human games.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Inventing the tasks: Absolute Zero and what bounds every loop
question: An Absolute Zero proposer writes a program that calls random.random() and returns the result. What happens to this proposal?
options: It becomes a hard abduction task, so the proposer gets a high learnability reward
It fails validation (random is a forbidden module, and two runs would give different outputs anyway), so it counts as a formatting error with reward -1
The solver gets credit for any numeric answer between 0 and 1
It is accepted, but only as an induction task
explain: Absolute Zero only accepts deterministic programs: it bans modules such as random and datetime outright, and it also runs each program twice (j = 2) and compares outputs. Only proposals that produce valid triplets count as correctly formatted, so this one gets the -1 penalty, which teaches the proposer to avoid unverifiable tasks.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Provider prompt caching is a different thing from semantic caching
question: You add the user's name and the current time to the very top of the system prompt to personalize replies. What happens to the two caches?
options: Prompt caching stops working because the prefix now differs per request; the semantic cache is unaffected if it embeds only the user's question
Both stop working
Neither is affected
The semantic cache stops working; prompt caching is unaffected
explain: Prefix matching is exact from the first token, so a per-request value at the top breaks every reuse. Put stable content first and variable content last. A semantic cache keyed on the user's question does not see the system prompt, which is exactly why it needs scoping when the system prompt matters.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: IMDSv2: session tokens, PUT and a hop limit of 1
question: An attacker has remote code execution on an EC2 instance that requires IMDSv2 with a hop limit of 1. Can they read the role credentials?
options: No: the token requirement blocks them
No: the TTL of 1 drops the token
Only if the instance has a public IP address
Yes: code on the instance can send its own PUT, receive the token directly and use it
explain: IMDSv2 protects against requests relayed by something else (WAFs, proxies, SSRF, routers). Code running on the instance is exactly the legitimate client IMDS is built to serve. That is why role permissions must still follow least privilege.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Insecure deserialization: when loading data runs code
question: A Java service checks `if (!(obj instanceof Cart)) throw ...` right after `readObject()`. Why does this not stop a gadget chain?
options: instanceof is slow
The chain runs inside readObject, while the object graph is being built, before the check executes
Gadget chains only affect PHP
Cart must implement Externalizable
explain: Deserialization hooks run as each object is reconstructed. By the time readObject returns and your check runs, any side effect has already happened. Filters must act before construction, which is what ObjectInputFilter does.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Path traversal and safe path joins
question: What is the strongest design for a "download your invoice" endpoint?
options: Accept a file name and strip every dot and slash
Accept an invoice ID, check the user owns it, look up the stored path server-side, and never put user text in a path
Accept a full path but only allow paths ending in .pdf
Accept a file name and URL-decode it twice before checking
explain: If user input never reaches the filesystem API, there is nothing to traverse, and the ownership check also closes the IDOR hole from the access-control course. Extension checks and character stripping are both known to be bypassable.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: LM programs: why the runtime should see the whole program
question: Why does the interpreter send the shared prefix to the runtime before the fork branches?
options: So that the prefix is computed and inserted into the radix tree once; branches arriving together would otherwise each find nothing cached and each prefill it
Because the runtime cannot accept prompts longer than the prefix
To let the runtime pick a different model for each branch
Because RadixAttention only works when requests arrive one at a time
explain: If both branches arrive at the same moment with nothing cached, each matches zero tokens and each computes the shared part. The paper calls the fix a frontend hint: it simplifies runtime matching and is one of the co-design benefits in its ablation.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Turning a road map into a weighted directed graph
question: In the toy graph, a planner picks the route with the fewest roads and breaks ties arbitrarily. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing; fewest roads always means fastest when weights are minutes
It may return S, C, F, T (14 min) even though S, D, F, T takes 9 min
It cannot find any route, because BFS ignores weights entirely
It always returns the slowest 3-road route
explain: Three routes tie at 3 roads (9, 10 and 14 minutes). Hop count ignores weights, so any of them can come out. We need an algorithm that compares accumulated minutes, which is exactly what Dijkstra's algorithm does.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Real engines: turn costs, live traffic and time-dependent travel
question: A travel time function says: leave at 08:05 and arrive at 08:30.6, or leave at 08:10 and arrive at 08:27.4. What does this violate, and why does it matter?
options: Admissibility; A* would overestimate
Nonnegative weights; travel times went negative
FIFO; waiting would beat leaving now, which breaks the label-setting search for earliest arrival
Turn restrictions; the profile is missing a penalty
explain: Leaving later and arriving earlier violates FIFO. Then arriving at a node as early as possible no longer guarantees arriving as early as possible further along, so a settled earliest-arrival label can be wrong. Dijkstra-style time-dependent search assumes FIFO, and the survey notes that other settings are studied separately.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: IIR filters, zero-phase filtering and real sensor data
question: A drone's control loop needs a filtered gyro reading every 1 ms. Someone proposes `sosfiltfilt` because it has zero phase delay. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; zero phase is ideal for control
sosfiltfilt only works on FIR filters
sosfiltfilt runs the filter backward from the end of the signal, so it needs future samples and cannot run in real time
sosfiltfilt halves the filter order, so it filters too weakly
explain: The backward pass starts from the last sample, which a real-time loop does not have yet. Real-time systems must use a causal filter (sosfilt, or an FIR) and accept or compensate its delay. Forward-backward filtering doubles the effective order; it does not halve it.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Masks instead of branches: compares, blends and AVX-512
question: In AVX-512, `r = _mm512_mask_add_ps(src, k, a, b)` with k = 0x0003. What are lanes 0 and 5 of r?
options: Lane 0 = a0 + b0, lane 5 = 0
Lane 0 = src0, lane 5 = a5 + b5
Both lanes are a + b; k only affects stores
Lane 0 = a0 + b0, lane 5 = src5
explain: 0x0003 sets bits 0 and 1, so lanes 0 and 1 get a + b. The mask_ form is merge masking: inactive lanes copy src. The maskz_ form would have produced 0 in lane 5.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: Why a general-purpose heap wastes memory
question: Why does a program not simply call `mmap` for every 24-byte object?
options: mmap cannot return memory smaller than a page, and each call is a system call, so it is both wasteful and slow
mmap memory cannot be written to until it is passed through malloc
mmap always returns memory on a different NUMA node
mmap regions are freed automatically after one function returns
explain: mmap works in whole pages (4 KiB on typical x86-64) and costs a kernel entry per call. An allocator amortizes both costs by carving many small objects out of one mapping. (A NUMA node, a group of CPUs with its own local memory on a non-uniform memory access machine, has nothing to do with it.)

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Three modules, one loop: how slime is laid out
question: You want to raise SGLang's KV cache budget inside a slime run. SGLang's own flag is `--mem-fraction-static`. What do you pass to slime's train.py?
options: `--sglang-mem-fraction-static 0.8`
`--mem-fraction-static 0.8`, since slime forwards unknown flags
Nothing: slime fixes SGLang memory internally
`--rollout-mem-fraction 0.8`
explain: SGLang arguments are passed through with a `--sglang-` prefix. Unprefixed flags are interpreted as Megatron or slime arguments, and there is no slime-specific rollout memory flag.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Fully async rollout and the price of staleness
question: A teammate enables fully async rollout on a colocated 8-GPU job and sees no speedup. Why?
options: Fully async only works with PPO
The default --sglang-server-concurrency is too low
With colocation rollout and training share GPUs and must take turns, so there are no independent resources to overlap
Fully async requires delta weight sync
explain: The docs say fully async needs separate GPUs for meaningful overlap. On shared GPUs the phases still alternate, so the async bound does not apply.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Verdicts, severity and priority: true, false and benign positives
question: A rule detects `vssadmin delete shadows`. It fires because the backup product deletes old shadow copies every night at 01:00, exactly as configured. What is the verdict, and what is the fix?
options: False positive; delete the rule
True positive; escalate to incident response
Benign true positive; record the backup schedule and add a narrow, documented exception for that product's signed process at that time
Undetermined; leave it open
explain: The rule saw exactly what it was built to see, so it is not a false positive. The activity is legitimate, so it is not an attack. The fix is context: a narrow exception tied to the backup product, not deleting a rule that catches ransomware precursors.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Malware on an endpoint: reading a process tree
question: Four parent and child pairs appear in today's EDR data. Which deserves the fastest look?
options: explorer.exe starting WINWORD.EXE
explorer.exe starting chrome.exe
explorer.exe starting Teams.exe
WINWORD.EXE starting powershell.exe -EncodedCommand
explain: The first three are a user launching ordinary applications from the desktop. A word processor launching an encoded PowerShell command is a classic sign of a malicious document.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: When to escalate, and case notes someone else can act on
question: Which case-note summary lets an incident lead act fastest?
options: "Weird stuff on a laptop, see the logs"
"Malware alert. Ran some queries. Looks bad."
"FIN-LT-042 ran a malicious macro at 09:15 UTC; an unknown device signed in as the user at 09:41. Host isolated, sessions revoked. Need IR to scope the account's access."
A copy of the full raw logs with no summary
explain: It states what happened, when, to what, how sure, what is already done and what is needed. The others force the reader to redo the triage.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Security is a secondary task: why people work around it
question: A company forces monthly password changes. An audit finds many passwords on sticky notes. What does Adams and Sasse's study suggest is the main cause?
options: Employees are careless and need stricter penalties
Sticky notes are too easy to buy
The policy demands more memorisation than people can manage, so they write passwords down to cope
Monthly changes are too infrequent
explain: Their respondents linked writing passwords down directly to forced changes and to having many passwords. Penalties do not reduce the memory load; changing the policy does.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a pretext: how manipulation is built and broken
question: A caller claiming to be from IT gives a callback number 'in case we get cut off'. What should the employee do to verify the caller?
options: Call the number given, since that proves the caller answers it
Ask the caller three questions only real IT staff would know
Look up the service desk in the company directory and call that number instead
Check that caller ID shows the company's name
explain: A number supplied by the caller leads back to the caller. Caller ID and display names are set by the caller too. Only a number from a source the caller does not control, such as the directory, verifies anything.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Designing help-desk verification that holds under pressure
question: Which change most reduces the number of risky judgement calls the help desk has to make at all?
options: Longer calls with more personal questions
Self-service recovery that requires an existing strong factor, such as a passkey
Allowing resets by email
Publishing the help desk's verification questions
explain: If most people can recover by proving a factor they still hold, only the rare cases with no factor left reach an agent, and those can get the slow, strong checks.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Badges, readers and tailgating
question: A log shows badge B22 exiting the lab at 08:50 with no entry by B22 that day. What is the most likely explanation to check first?
options: The badge reader's clock is wrong
B22 cloned someone else's card
B22 followed someone into the lab without badging (tailgating or piggybacking)
B22 works from home
explain: An exit with no matching entry is the classic trace of tailgating. Confirm with CCTV and a conversation, and look at whether the door-held alarm fired around the time B22 must have entered.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: A reporting culture, and what to do when someone is fooled
question: After a tailgater is spotted in a restricted area, what should be preserved first?
options: The visitor sign-in sheet only
Nothing, as the person has left
CCTV footage and badge logs, before they are overwritten
The door hardware
explain: Recordings and logs often roll over after a set period. They show who entered, when, and where they went, including near network ports and unlocked screens.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Training at scale: dead latents and feature splitting
question: You compare a 4,096-latent and a 65,536-latent SAE on the same layer. The smaller one has a 'Python code' latent; the larger has several latents for different Python contexts and none that matches it exactly. What does this indicate?
options: The larger SAE is broken
Feature splitting: the wider dictionary covers the same concept at finer resolution
The smaller SAE has dead latents
Python is not represented in the model
explain: This is the expected pattern from Towards Monosemanticity: wider dictionaries refine broad latents into families of more specific ones.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Ordinary kriging: solving for the best weights
question: The ordinary kriging system has an extra row of ones and an extra unknown $\mu$. What would go wrong if you dropped them and just solved $\Gamma \boldsymbol\lambda = \boldsymbol\gamma_0$?
options: The weights would no longer be forced to sum to 1, so the estimate would be biased whenever the unknown mean is not zero
Nothing; the row only speeds up the solve
The estimate would ignore the nearest sensor
The matrix would become 8 by 8
explain: The constraint row enforces $\sum_i \lambda_i = 1$, which makes the estimate unbiased for any constant mean. Without it the weights can sum to anything, and the estimate is pulled toward or away from zero.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Draft, verify, keep: the loop with greedy decoding
question: Why does the target pass produce gamma + 1 distributions rather than gamma?
options: Causal attention gives a next-token distribution after every input token, including after the last guess, which supplies a bonus token when all guesses pass
One extra position is needed to check the prefix
The draft also returns one distribution that is reused
It is an implementation detail that is never used
explain: The forward pass over prefix plus gamma guesses outputs a distribution after each of them. The last one, after guess gamma, is a free target prediction used only when all guesses are accepted, raising the maximum to gamma + 1 tokens per round.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: EAGLE drafts, prompt lookup, and speculation in vLLM
question: Medusa's typical acceptance, Medusa-2, EAGLE-2 and prompt lookup: which of these can change the output distribution compared to the original target model?
options: Only EAGLE-2
Typical acceptance and Medusa-2
Prompt lookup, because copied tokens skip the target
All four
explain: Typical acceptance replaces rejection sampling with a threshold, and Medusa-2 fine-tunes the backbone itself. EAGLE-2 and prompt lookup only change how drafts are proposed; verification with the standard rule keeps the target's distribution.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Long audio, streaming and hallucinations in production
question: In Whisper-Streaming you raise MinChunkSize, the minimum new audio processed per update. What happens?
options: Latency rises, but each update sees more audio, so quality tends to improve
Latency drops, because fewer updates are needed
Nothing, because LocalAgreement only depends on text
WER rises, because the 30 s window overflows
explain: The paper describes MinChunkSize as the parameter that controls latency and quality. Bigger chunks mean waiting longer before each update, but each transcription has more context. The paper also found the computationally unaware latency (ignoring compute time) to be about twice the chunk size, since two consecutive updates must agree. Buffers are trimmed at sentence ends to stay near 30 s, so overflow is not the issue.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Walking an x86-64 page table, bit by bit
question: A program maps 1 GiB of memory and touches all of it with 4 KiB pages. Roughly how much memory do the last-level page tables alone take?
options: 4 KiB
64 KiB
2 MiB
1 GiB
explain: 1 GiB / 4 KiB = 262,144 page-table entries at 8 bytes each = 2 MiB, which is 512 PTE tables of 4 KiB. With 2 MiB pages the same gigabyte needs just 512 PMD entries, one 4 KiB table.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Steering by adding a vector to the residual stream
question: Why can a vector added only at layer l change the model's next-token prediction?
options: Because the model recomputes all earlier layers after the addition
Because the residual stream is a running sum: later layers read the shifted stream and the unembedding reads its final value
Because the vector is also added to the weights of every later layer
It cannot; the vector must be added at the last layer to matter
explain: Each block adds its output to the stream it reads, so a vector added at layer l stays in the sum. Later attention and MLP layers read it and react to it, and the final stream is what the unembedding decodes. No weights change and earlier layers are not rerun.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Side effects and how to evaluate a steering vector
question: Your refusal-steered model keeps its MMLU score, yet users report rambling, repetitive answers. Which check would have caught this?
options: Raising the coefficient
Measuring loss or KL on ordinary prompts and reading open-ended generations, not just multiple-choice accuracy
Running MMLU with more subjects
Using a single contrast pair instead of many
explain: MMLU in the A/B format reads one token's probability, which can survive while generation quality collapses. CAA saw exactly this: multiple-choice capability held while larger multipliers degraded open-ended text. Loss on ordinary text, KL on unrelated prompts and reading samples catch it.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Online filtering: EMA as a low-pass, Welford for anomaly flags
question: Two parallel tasks each computed Welford state for half of a sensor's readings. Can you get the exact overall variance?
options: No, variance needs all raw values in one place
Yes, by averaging the two variances
Yes, by combining (n, mean, M2) of both halves with a pairwise merge formula
Only if both halves have the same mean
explain: Averaging variances ignores the difference between the two means. Chan, Golub and LeVeque give a merge: M2 = M2a + M2b + delta squared x na x nb / (na + nb), with delta the difference of means. This is what makes mean and variance easy to parallelize across partitions.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Causal masks, teacher forcing and cross-attention
question: In encoder-decoder (cross) attention, where do the queries, keys and values come from?
options: Queries, keys and values all come from the encoder output
Queries from the encoder; keys and values from the decoder
Queries from the decoder; keys and values from the encoder output
Queries and keys from the decoder; values from the encoder
explain: The decoder is asking questions about the source, so it supplies the queries. The encoder output supplies the keys (what each source position offers) and the values (what gets copied). This lets every decoder position attend over all input positions.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: One layer end to end, in numbers and in code, and how it decodes
question: A position's sum x + Sublayer(x) is (2, 4, 6). What does LayerNorm output with gain 1, bias 0 and a negligible epsilon?
options: (2, 4, 6) divided by its length: about (0.27, 0.53, 0.80)
(-2, 0, 2), the vector minus its mean
About (-1.22, 0, 1.22): subtract the mean 4, divide by the standard deviation 1.63
(0, 0.5, 1), rescaled to the range 0 to 1
explain: The mean is 4 and the variance is (4 + 0 + 4)/3 = 8/3, so the standard deviation is 1.63. (2 - 4)/1.63 = -1.22, and so on. LayerNorm centers and scales by the standard deviation; dividing by the length is a different normalization, and subtracting the mean alone leaves the scale untouched.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Term-frequency saturation: what k1 controls
question: A product search team sees titles like "usb cable usb-c usb charger usb" outranking clean titles for the query usb. Which change to k1 most directly reduces the benefit of repeating a word?
options: Increase k1 from 1.2 to 5
Set b to 0
Decrease k1 from 1.2 to about 0.5
Leave k1, since BM25 already ignores repeats
explain: Lower k1 makes the factor saturate sooner, so the second and later copies add less. Raising k1 does the opposite. b controls length normalization, not repetition. BM25 does not ignore repeats; with k1 = 1.2 the fourth copy still adds weight.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Causal self-attention: each position may only look backward
question: Why does nanoGPT compute q, k and v for all 12 heads with one 768-to-2304 Linear instead of 36 small ones?
options: It is mathematically different and gives better accuracy
GPT-2 heads share their key matrices
It halves the parameter count
One large matrix multiply uses the GPU far better than many small ones, and gives the same result
explain: Stacking the per-head projection matrices side by side is the same linear map, so the outputs are identical. The gain is purely efficiency: one large matmul instead of many small launches. Parameter count is the same 768 x 2304 weights either way.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Training it: initialization, AdamW and a warmup plus cosine schedule
question: A friend's character-level model reaches 1.3 val loss and a colleague's BPE model 2.9. Which is better?
options: They cannot be compared: one is nats per character, the other nats per token
The character model, since 1.3 is lower
The BPE model, since 2.9 is higher
They are equal after dividing by ln 2
explain: Cross-entropy is measured per token, and the two tokenizers define different tokens over the same text. To compare you would need a per-character or per-byte measure on the same data.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: A derivative is the slope you see when you zoom in
question: A loss $L(w)$ has derivative $L'(w) = -4$ at the current weight. Which small change to $w$ lowers the loss?
options: Decrease w, because the derivative is negative
Increase w slightly: the slope is negative, so L falls as w grows
Neither: a negative derivative means you are at a minimum
Any change, because the loss is already decreasing over time
explain: A negative slope means $L$ goes down as $w$ goes up, so a small increase in $w$ lowers $L$ by about $4$ times the step. A minimum is where the derivative is zero, not negative.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Gradient descent: walking downhill and choosing the step size
question: Training loss is going down very slowly and smoothly, and you know the gradients are correct. Which change most directly speeds things up?
options: Increase the learning rate moderately and watch for oscillation
Flip the sign of the update so you move along the gradient
Decrease the learning rate
Stop training; slow progress means a minimum was reached
explain: Smooth, slow decrease is the signature of a learning rate that is too small (like $\eta = 0.05$ here). Raise it gradually; if the loss starts to oscillate or climb you have passed the stable limit. Moving along the gradient would increase the loss.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Files, paths and permissions: finding your way around
question: You run `chmod 044 notes.txt` on a file you own, giving `----r--r--`, then `cat notes.txt` as yourself. What happens?
options: It prints the file, since everyone else can read it
It prints the file, because owners can always read their own files
chmod fails, because the owner must keep read permission
Permission denied, because only the owner bits apply to you
explain: The kernel picks one class: you own the file, so only the owner bits (`---`) count, and the group and others bits are ignored. A real run prints `cat: notes.txt: Permission denied`. You can still `chmod 644` it back, because changing the mode needs ownership, not read permission.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: File descriptors: why the order of 2>&1 matters
question: `grep -c error app.log > count.txt` prints `grep: app.log: No such file or directory` on the terminal. Why is that message not in count.txt?
options: count.txt is opened only after grep succeeds
grep prints errors through the shell, not through a file descriptor
Error messages go to fd 2, and only fd 1 was redirected
Redirection is ignored when the command fails
explain: The shell opens count.txt on fd 1 before exec, whether or not grep succeeds (so count.txt now exists, empty). grep writes its complaint to fd 2, which still points at the terminal.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Your environment and remote machines: dotfiles, ssh and tmux
question: Which approach keeps a 3-hour job running if your ssh connection to the server drops?
options: Starting it as `./job.sh &` in the ssh session
Starting it inside tmux on your laptop, then running ssh in that tmux
Adding `set -e` to job.sh
Starting it in a tmux session on the server, then detaching
explain: The tmux server on the remote machine owns the shell, so losing the connection only detaches a client. With `&` alone the job stays a job of the login shell, which forwards SIGHUP. tmux on the laptop protects only the laptop side: the ssh connection and the remote shell still die. `nohup ./job.sh &` would also survive.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Negative sampling: one word2vec update by hand
question: Why is SGNS so much cheaper per training pair than the full softmax?
options: It uses smaller vectors
It skips the input vector update
It only trains on frequent words
It touches $k + 1$ output vectors instead of all $W$
explain: The softmax normalizer needs every output vector; the negative sampling objective needs only the true context and the k samples. With k = 5 and W = 1,000,000 that is 6 dot products instead of a million.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Embeddings for IDs: categorical features, hashing and weight tying
question: A language model has a 50,000-word vocabulary and $d = 768$. How many parameters does tying the input embedding and the output softmax matrix save?
explain: Each matrix is 50,000 x 768 = 38,400,000 numbers; tying keeps one of them. (76.8 million is the size of both together.)

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Inside a GPU: many small cores fed by one big memory
question: A kernel is launched with only 20 thread blocks on an A100 (108 SMs), one block per SM at a time. What is the most likely problem?
options: HBM capacity is exceeded
Most SMs have no work, so the GPU is underused regardless of memory speed
The warps are too large, so threads diverge
The L2 cache is too small to hold 20 blocks
explain: Each thread block runs on one SM, so 20 blocks occupy at most 20 of 108 SMs. NVIDIA's guide recommends launching several times more blocks than SMs. This is a latency or parallelism limit, not a memory capacity issue.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: From hello.c to a running process
question: You split a program into `main.c` and `util.c`. `main.c` calls `parse()` defined in `util.c`. Which stage is the first one that needs to see both files?
options: The preprocessor, because it must find parse()
The compiler, because it must check parse() exists
The assembler, because it encodes the call instruction
The linker, because it resolves the call to parse() across object files
explain: Each .c file is preprocessed, compiled and assembled on its own; a declaration of `parse` (usually from a header) is enough for the compiler. The call is left as an undefined symbol plus a relocation in main.o. The linker is the first stage that sees both object files and patches the real address in.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Where a program's memory lives: code, heap and stack
question: Right after `call square` executes, which statement is true?
options: rsp increased by 8 and the program counter points at square
rsp is unchanged; the return address is kept in a special register
rsp decreased by 8, the stack top holds the address of the instruction after the call, and the program counter points at square
rsp decreased by 8 and the stack top holds the address of square
explain: The stack grows down, so a push subtracts 8 from rsp. call pushes the return address (the next instruction in the caller), not the target, then jumps by writing square's address into the program counter.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Virtual memory: every process gets its own addresses
question: Why does x86-64 use a 4-level tree instead of one flat table indexed by the 36-bit page number?
options: A flat table cannot be cached in the TLB
Flat tables cannot hold physical frame numbers
Hardware cannot index arrays larger than 512 entries
A flat table would need 2^36 entries x 8 bytes = 512 GiB per process, mostly describing unused memory
explain: 2^36 x 8 bytes = 512 GiB (a gibibyte is 2^30 bytes), for every process. A tree only allocates the lower-level tables for regions actually in use, so a small process needs a few pages of page tables. The cost is the longer walk, which the TLB hides.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Supervised fine-tuning: same loss, curated data, masked prompt
question: Why must the end-of-sequence token after the answer be included in the trained targets?
options: It carries the reward signal for RLHF
It is required by the softmax
Otherwise the model never learns when to stop and keeps generating
It prevents the prompt from being masked
explain: Stopping is a learned prediction like any other. If the end token is masked, the model never sees a gradient for ending its turn and tends to run on, for example by writing the next user turn itself.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: RL with PPO: maximize reward, stay close to the SFT model
question: In a PPO minibatch, a token has advantage -0.5 and its ratio has fallen to 0.7, with epsilon 0.2. What does this token contribute to the gradient?
options: A push to lower its probability further, because its advantage is negative
A push to raise its probability back to 1
Nothing, because negative advantages are always clipped
Nothing: the clipped term -0.4 is the minimum and does not depend on the weights
explain: rho x A = -0.35 and clip(0.7, 0.8, 1.2) x A = -0.4. The min is the clipped -0.4, a constant, so no gradient flows: the token was already made 30 percent less likely, past the 20 percent PPO allows per batch. If its ratio had been 1.3 instead, the unclipped -0.65 would be the min and the gradient would push it back down.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Answering AND queries by merging postings
question: Why does the engine keep df in the in-memory dictionary even for a pure Boolean search engine?
options: Boolean retrieval multiplies scores by df
It lets the planner order terms by list length before reading any postings
The merge algorithm needs df to know when to stop
It is needed to decompress postings
explain: Knowing each list's length up front lets the query optimizer intersect the shortest lists first. The merge itself stops when either pointer runs off its list, so it never needs df.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: C in one sitting: types, operators, control flow and functions
options: two three
two
one two three
two three other
explain: switch jumps to case 2, then falls through into case 3 because nothing stops it, and the break after three leaves the switch before default. Forgetting break is a classic bug; when fallthrough is intended, write a comment saying so.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Arrays, pointer arithmetic and strings
question: `char a[] = "cat", b[] = "cat";` Does `if (a == b)` take the branch?
options: Yes, the two strings hold the same characters
It does not compile
Only if the compiler merges identical strings
No: == compares the addresses of two different arrays; use strcmp(a, b) == 0
explain: Both arrays decay to pointers to their first elements, and two distinct arrays never share an address, so the comparison is false; clang even warns `array comparison always evaluates to false`. strcmp compares the characters and returns 0 when they match.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Function pointers and void *: writing generic code like qsort
question: What does `int *f(int);` declare, compared with `int (*f)(int);`?
options: Both declare a pointer to a function returning int
The first is a pointer to an int, the second a function
Both declare a function returning a pointer
The first declares a function returning int *; the second, a pointer to a function returning int
explain: Without parentheses, `()` binds to f first, so f is a function (taking int) that returns `int *`. With `(*f)`, f is first a pointer, and what it points to is a function taking int and returning int.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Rust for C programmers: cargo, let, structs, enums and match
question: You add a variant `Triangle { b: f64, h: f64 }` to `Shape` but do not touch `area`. What happens?
options: `area` returns 0.0 for a triangle, the default for an unmatched value
It compiles with a warning and panics when a triangle reaches the match
The match falls through to the next arm, as a C switch without break does
rustc rejects the program with E0004, because the match no longer covers every variant
explain: Matches are exhaustive and checked at compile time. Adding a variant makes every match on the type that lacks it (and lacks a `_` arm) a compile error, which points you at each place that needs a decision. There is no default value and no fall-through.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Ownership in methods and loops: self, &self, &mut self and for
question: `v` is a `Vec<String>` with three elements. Which line compiles on its own?
options: `let s = v[1];`
`for s in v {}` followed by `println!("{}", v.len());`
`let s: &String = &v[1];`
`let first = &v[0]; v.push(String::new()); println!("{first}");`
explain: Borrowing an element is fine. Option 1 is E0507 (cannot move out of an index). Option 2 is E0382, because the loop consumed `v`. Option 4 is E0502: `first` is still used after `push` needs `&mut v`.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: When the checker says no: clone, Rc and RefCell
question: A tree where each child needs a pointer back to its parent, and nodes are created and removed while the program runs. Which choice fits best?
options: Plain `&Node` references stored in each child
`Rc` from parent to children and `Weak` from child to parent (with `RefCell` where nodes must change)
Clone the parent into each child
explain: Nodes have no single owner whose scope covers every use, which is what plain references need. Cloning would give each child a separate copy rather than the real parent. `Rc` counts owners; a `Weak` back-pointer does not count, so parent and child do not keep each other alive in a cycle that leaks. `RefCell` allows mutation, checked at run time. This is the Book's tree design.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A matrix is a function that moves every vector
question: $A$ has shape $3 \times 5$. Which input can it multiply, and what comes out?
options: A vector with 5 components; out comes a vector with 3
A vector with 3 components; out comes a vector with 5
Any vector; out comes a 3 x 5 matrix
A vector with 15 components; out comes a scalar
explain: Each row has 5 entries and is dotted with $\mathbf{x}$, so $\mathbf{x}$ needs 5 components. There are 3 rows, so 3 output components. An $m \times n$ matrix maps $\mathbb{R}^n$ to $\mathbb{R}^m$.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Orthogonality, projections and least squares
question: After a least-squares fit, the residual is $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{y} - X\mathbf{w}$. Which statement must hold?
options: r is the zero vector
r points in the same direction as y
r is orthogonal to every column of X
r has the same length as y
explain: The best fit is the projection of $\mathbf{y}$ onto the column space, so the leftover is perpendicular to that space: $X^\top\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{0}$. It is zero only if $\mathbf{y}$ was already reachable, which a tall noisy system almost never is.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Loss: turning "fits the data" into one number
question: A classifier gives the correct class probability 0.9 on one example and 0.1 on another. Roughly how do their cross-entropy losses compare?
options: The 0.1 example costs about 22 times more (2.303 vs 0.105)
They are equal, since both are 0.4 away from 0.5
The 0.1 example costs exactly 9 times more
The 0.9 example costs more because it is more confident
explain: Cross-entropy is $-\ln p$: $-\ln 0.9 = 0.105$ and $-\ln 0.1 = 2.303$, a ratio of about 22. The log makes the cost grow without bound as the probability of the right answer goes to 0, which is exactly the confident-wrong case.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Overfitting: when the training loss lies
question: You can't change the degree-9 model. Which change most directly reduces its overfitting?
options: Train longer to reach exactly zero training loss
Collect more training data from the same distribution
Evaluate on the training set instead
Increase the learning rate
explain: More data constrains the same model: median test RMS fell from 0.643 at N = 10 to 0.340 at N = 100. Training longer only drives it further into the noise, and evaluating on training data hides the problem.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Measuring a model: metrics, thresholds and cross-validation
question: You ran 5-fold cross-validation to choose lambda, picked the best value, and want to report expected performance. What should you report?
options: The mean cross-validation score of the chosen lambda
The best single fold's score
The training score of the final model
The score on a test set that was never used for choosing lambda
explain: The chosen lambda won partly by luck on those folds, so its cross-validation score is optimistic. The scikit-learn guide keeps a test set aside for exactly this final evaluation.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: What hidden units compute: hinges, cuts and new features
question: Connect-the-dots approximation of $\sin x$ gave worst errors 0.21, 0.070 and 0.019 with 4, 8 and 16 equal pieces. Roughly how many pieces give a worst error near 0.005?
explain: Each doubling cut the error by about 3 to 4 times, and the ratio was heading toward 4. One more doubling, to 32 pieces, gives about 0.0048. 64 would overshoot to around 0.0012.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Multi-class outputs: softmax, logits and the p minus y gradient
question: A 10-class network gives the true class probability 0.98 and some wrong class probability 0.015. What are $\partial L/\partial z$ for those two logits?
options: 0 and 0, because the prediction is already right
explain: $\partial L/\partial z_j = p_j - \delta_{yj}$. True class: 0.98 - 1 = -0.02, a small push up. Wrong class: 0.015 - 0 = 0.015, a small push down. Confident correct predictions produce small gradients, but never exactly zero.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Training a real network: an MLP on handwritten digits
question: Training loss keeps falling, but validation loss has stopped falling and is slowly rising. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Train for many more epochs until validation loss falls again
Report test accuracy at every epoch and pick the best one
Increase the model size
Stop at the epoch with the lowest validation loss (early stopping) or add regularisation
explain: Rising validation loss with falling training loss is the signature of overfitting. Early stopping or weight decay from the ML fundamentals course address it. Picking the epoch by test accuracy leaks the test set into model selection.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Beyond physical memory: page faults, swapping and replacement
question: A database scans a 50-page table in a loop, over and over, and has 49 frames for it. Which replacement policy gives the best hit rate?
options: LRU, because it keeps recently used pages
FIFO, because the scan is in arrival order
Random, because LRU and FIFO always evict the page needed next and hit 0% of the time
All three give the same hit rate
explain: In a loop larger than the cache, the least recently used page is exactly the one the loop needs next, so LRU (and FIFO, which evicts in the same order here) misses on every access. Random sometimes keeps the right pages and gets a non-zero hit rate. OPT would do better still.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Concurrency bugs: atomicity, ordering and deadlock
question: Thread A starts thread B and then sets `cfg = load_config()`. Thread B begins by reading `cfg->port`. It crashes occasionally. What kind of bug is this, and what is the usual fix?
options: An atomicity violation; wrap the read of cfg->port in a lock
An order violation; make B wait on a condition variable until A sets a flag after loading cfg
A deadlock; acquire locks in a global order
A data race on port; declare cfg volatile
explain: B assumes A's assignment has already happened: the intended order is not enforced. A lock alone does not fix it, since B could still take the lock first and see NULL. B must wait for a state variable (set by A after loading) using a condition variable, as in OSTEP's Mozilla fix. volatile does not create ordering.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Crash consistency: fsck and journaling
question: In data journaling, why must the file system wait for TxB, I[v2], B[v2] and Db to finish before writing TxE, instead of issuing all five writes at once?
options: Because the disk can only accept one write at a time
Because TxE must be written to the final location, not the journal
Because the disk may reorder a large write; TxE could land before Db, and replay would then copy garbage as if it were committed
Because waiting makes the journal smaller
explain: Disks schedule writes internally. If all five are issued together, TxE might hit the disk while Db has not. After a crash the transaction looks committed, and recovery would checkpoint garbage. Writing TxE only after the rest completes, as an atomic 512-byte write, closes the window.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Joint and marginal distributions, and the chain rule of probability
question: A language model gives probabilities 0.2, 0.5 and 0.1 to three successive tokens, each conditioned on the tokens before it. What is the total log-probability (natural log) of the three tokens?
options: About -4.61, the sum of the three logs, equal to ln 0.01
About -1.54, the average of the three logs
0.8, the sum of the three probabilities
About -2.30, the log of the smallest probability
explain: By the chain rule the joint probability is 0.2 x 0.5 x 0.1 = 0.01, and the log of a product is the sum of logs: -1.61 - 0.69 - 2.30 = -4.61. The average, -1.54 per token, is minus the cross-entropy per token used as a training loss.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Estimating parameters from data: maximum likelihood
question: A language model assigns probability 0.5 to every correct next token in a validation set. What is its average cross-entropy (natural log), and what does minimizing it on training data correspond to?
options: 0.5; minimizing the error rate
About 0.693; maximizing the likelihood of the training tokens
About 0.693; minimizing the variance of the predictions
1.0; maximizing accuracy
explain: Cross-entropy averages -log of the probability given to the correct token: -ln 0.5 = 0.693. Minimizing average negative log-likelihood over the training data is exactly maximum likelihood estimation of the model's parameters.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Power and sample size: planning an A/B test before running it
question: A test has 30% power for the smallest effect you care about, and it comes out significant. What is the main risk in the reported lift?
options: It is probably too small, since low power biases estimates toward 0
There is none: a significant result is trustworthy whatever the power
It is likely exaggerated, since only lucky overestimates cross the threshold in a weak test
The false positive rate has risen to 70%
explain: With low power, the runs that reach significance are mostly the ones where noise inflated the estimate, so the significant estimate overstates the truth (the exaggeration ratio). Alpha, the false positive rate, does not depend on power.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Run your own scaling study: sweep, fit, extrapolate, error bars
question: At one budget your sweep trained only models smaller than the optimum, so the losses fall steadily and never turn up. What happens if you fit a parabola in $\log N$ to them?
options: The vertex lands on the optimum, because a parabola extrapolates the valley exactly
The fit raises an error, so you will notice the problem
Nothing; Approach 2 does not depend on which sizes you train
The vertex is extrapolated off one wall of a valley that is not exactly parabolic, so it can be biased
explain: In our repeated studies, sizes from 1/64x to 1x of the optimum pulled Approach 2's median forecast down to 75B against a truth of 96B, with no error raised. Approach 3, which fits the full formula to all runs, was not biased. Bracket each valley on both sides.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Inference cost, overtraining and where scaling laws break
question: A team will serve its model to millions of users for a year and needs a fixed quality bar. What does inference-aware scaling recommend?
options: Train the Chinchilla-optimal model, since it reaches the bar with the least compute
Train a smaller model on more tokens than Chinchilla-optimal, paying extra training compute to cut serving cost
Train the largest model the budget allows on fewer tokens, since bigger models are more sample-efficient
Train any size; inference cost does not depend on model size
explain: Serving costs about 2N FLOPs per token, so with heavy usage a smaller model that reaches the same loss by training longer has lower lifetime cost. Chinchilla-optimal minimizes training compute only. Bigger-and-shorter is Kaplan's advice and makes serving more expensive.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Comparing systems honestly: judgment holes, variance, online tests
question: B beats A on MAP, 0.43 versus 0.37, over 8 queries. B wins on 2 queries and loses on 6. Which conclusion is justified?
options: B is better: MAP is the standard measure
Not established yet: check per-query differences with a paired test and add queries
A is better because it wins more queries
They are identical because 8 queries is too few to compute MAP
explain: A mean driven by one or two queries is fragile, and with 8 queries neither a t-test (p = 0.44) nor a sign test (p = 0.29) supports a general claim. Counting wins alone is also not a valid conclusion. Use more queries (about 50 is a common minimum) and a paired test.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Where dense retrieval fails: hybrid search and re-ranking
question: A dense-only search works well on natural questions but users complain that searching an exact SKU (stock keeping unit, a product code) like `KX-4471-B` returns similar-looking but wrong products. What is the most targeted fix?
options: Increase the embedding dimension from 384 to 1024
Lower the softmax temperature at query time
Switch from cosine to dot product
Add BM25 in parallel and fuse the lists with RRF
explain: Rare exact identifiers are where lexical matching is strongest and dense vectors are weakest. Hybrid retrieval keeps the dense model's paraphrase handling and adds exact-term recall. Temperature is a training-time setting; more dimensions or another similarity function do not create exact-match behavior.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Byte-level BPE: how GPT-2 and its successors tokenize anything
question: Why can GPT-2's tokenizer encode an emoji it never saw during tokenizer training, without an unknown token?
options: It has a fallback table of every Unicode character
The regex deletes characters it does not recognise
It maps any unseen character to the nearest known one
The emoji is UTF-8 bytes, and all 256 byte values are base tokens, so it can always be written as bytes
